CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1

A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix

Four neurons read a day of weather and name its season; five read a pixel and name its colour. Each layer is one matrix, and applying it to the data is one product.

The data: days at Newark airport

The days of 2018 to 2021 are n = 1,457 points with m = 2 coordinates each. The first four:
      date  tmax_f  tmin_f
2018-01-01    20.1     6.3
2018-01-02    27.1    12.2
2018-01-03    30.2    10.2
  • The daily weather at Newark airport, 2006 to 2024. One point is one day, with m = 2 coordinates, its high and its low; the n = 1,457 days of 2018 to 2021 are the rows of one matrix, standardized as in meeting 10 with the means and the deviations of 2006 to 2017.
  • Each day carries a label, its season. Can four rules, one for each season, read the two numbers of a day and name its season?
CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix2 / 17

A neuron: a rule that reads a day

  • A neuron has one weight for each coordinate of the point and one more number, its bias. It multiplies each coordinate by its weight, adds the products and the bias, and the sum is its score. Four neurons, one for each season, read the same two numbers; the softmax after them turns the four scores into four probabilities.
  • Nobody chose these weights by hand: a program adjusted them in many small steps until the layer named the right season for as many days of 2006 to 2017 as it could. That is training.
Notes. Two minutes on the sketch: inputs, weights on the dendrites, the bias in the body, the score on the axon, the softmax. The numbers are those of the Fourth of July 2019, which the next slides compute.

One neuron, one day: the score by hand

s=w1x1+w2x2+b
Day 2019-07-04: high 89 °F, low 74 °F. Standardized: z = (1.31, 1.53).
The winter neuron: w = (-1.36, -1.97), b = -0.65.
Its score: -1.36 x 1.31 + (-1.97) x 1.53 + (-0.65) = -5.43
shape of w: (2,), shape of z: (2,); w @ z + b is one number.
  • The winter neuron on the Fourth of July: a large negative score. The neuron fires when s ≥ 0; this one does not.
  • With matrices, w and x are columns, m × 1, and s = wTx + b: the transpose writes w as a row, and a row times a column is one number, the sum of the products of matching entries. In NumPy both have one dimension, shape (2,), and w @ x + b is their dot product plus the bias.
Notes. The hand computation of the act: ask for the score before the third line is read. Three products, their sum, the bias.

Four neurons, one day: the weights are a matrix

s=Wx+b
W @ z + b, shape (4,): winter -5.43, spring +0.05, summer +4.18, fall +1.20
shape of W: (4, 2), shape of b: (4,)
The largest score is that of the summer neuron, at position 2: the argmax.
  • Row j of W holds the weights of neuron j. W is K × m = 4 × 2 and x is 2 × 1, so Wx is 4 × 1, and so is b: four scores in one line, W @ x + b. Nothing has to be repeated.
  • The answer of the layer is the neuron with the largest score: the position of the largest entry, its argmax.
Notes. A layer: a set of neurons that read the same point, stored as one matrix with one neuron in each row.
CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix5 / 17

From scores to probabilities: the softmax

pk=eskes1+es2+…+esK
def softmax_rows(S):
    shifted = S - S.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)       # the largest entry of every row becomes 0
    E = np.exp(shifted)
    return E / E.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

the four scores:        winter -5.43, spring +0.05, summer +4.18, fall +1.20
their probabilities:    winter 0.000, spring 0.015, summer 0.937, fall 0.048   (they add to 1.000)
sigmoid of each score:  winter 0.004, spring 0.513, summer 0.985, fall 0.769   (each entry by itself)
  • The K scores of a point become K positive numbers that add to 1, read as probabilities. Every probability depends on all the scores of the point: the softmax is a function of a row. On a matrix of scores it treats each row separately.
  • The sigmoid, σ(s) = 1 / (1 + e−s), is the other function of this unit. It acts on every entry by itself, replaces fires-or-not by a number between 0 and 1, and keeps the shape of its input. Its four numbers do not add to 1.
Notes. The function was written by an AI assistant to stated requirements; the full notebook has each group ask for its own. The largest entry of each row is subtracted first, so that no exponential is too large for the computer.

Four neurons, many days: one product

S_days = Z_days @ W_seasons.T + b_seasons        # the line of Step 4
S=XWT+1bT
shape of Z_days: (1457, 2)   shape of W_seasons.T: (2, 4)   shape of S_days: (1457, 4)
The largest score names the right season on 59.3% of the 1,457 days.
  • X is n × m and WT is m × K, so S is n × K: row i belongs to day i, column j to neuron j. W is transposed because a neuron is a row of W, and the product needs each neuron's weights as a column.
  • 1bT is the row of biases written again on every row: the mathematics needs the column of ones, and NumPy broadcasts + b, as it broadcast - mu in Act 0.
Notes. The line of the meeting. Say the two shapes aloud, and why the transpose moved to W.

The four cases

one point x, shape (m,)n points X, shape (n, m)
one neuron: w of shape (m,), b a numberw @ x + b is a numberX @ w + b has shape (n,); b is broadcast
K neurons: W of shape (K, m), b of shape (K,)W @ x + b has shape (K,)X @ W.T + b has shape (n, K); b is broadcast
  • The bias needs help exactly when there are many points: the mathematics writes a column of ones, and NumPy broadcasts.
  • The shapes do not always warn of a missing transpose: when K = m, X @ W + b runs, and its numbers are wrong.
  • The same four lines work on any data. The second example: the pixels of your group's image.
Notes. The table is the summary of the act. Review Quiz 11 asks for the shapes.

A point is now one pixel, with m = 3 coordinates: red, green, blue. image.reshape(-1, 3) writes the n = H × W pixels as the rows of X. The neuron with the weights 0.299, 0.587, 0.114 and the bias 0 reads every pixel, and its score is the brightness: the picture of the scores is the grey image of meeting 10.

A neuron that fires

b_bright = -s_grey.mean()                        # minus the mean brightness of the image
fires = X @ w_grey + b_bright >= 0               # True for the points on which the neuron fires
print(f"bias {b_bright:.3f}: the neuron fires on {fires.mean():.1%} of the {n:,} pixels")

bias -0.518: the neuron fires on 53.1% of the 320,640 pixels

A brightness is never negative, so with the bias 0 the grey neuron fires on every pixel. With the bias −(mean brightness) it fires on the pixels brighter than the average. θ = −b is the threshold of the neuron.

Five neurons, one for each reference colour

K = 5
C = reference_colours(X, K)              # K rows and 3 columns: the reference colours, darkest first
W = C.copy()                             # the weights of the layer: row j is reference colour j
b = -0.5 * (C ** 2).sum(axis=1)          # the biases of the layer: one number for each neuron

shape of W: (5, 3)   shape of b: (5,)
W =
[[0.32 0.36 0.31]
 [0.63 0.46 0.1 ]
 [0.53 0.53 0.45]
 [0.48 0.57 0.66]
 [0.67 0.65 0.55]]
b = [-0.16 -0.31 -0.38 -0.49 -0.59]

Five reference colours of the image, found by a method called k-means. Neuron j has the weights cj and the bias −½|cj|²: the largest score belongs to the neuron whose colour is nearest to the pixel. The layer names the colour of a pixel, as the layer of seasons named the season of a day.

Notes. Why the nearest colour wins: |x − c|² = x·x − 2(c·x − ½ c·c), and x·x is the same for every neuron. Review Quiz 11 asks the students for this argument; do not give it unless a group asks.

CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix13 / 17

Many neurons, many points: the three loops

def layer_loops(X, W, b):
    n, m = X.shape
    K = W.shape[0]
    S = np.empty((n, K))
    for i in range(n):                   # every point
        for j in range(K):               # every neuron
            total = b[j]
            for c in range(m):           # every coordinate
                total += W[j, c] * X[i, c]
            S[i, j] = total
    return S
  • S has n rows and K columns: row i belongs to pixel i, column j to neuron j. The loops compute it from the definition: every point, every neuron, every coordinate.
  • For the days, the same scores were one line: S = XWT + 1bT. In Colab you write that line for the pixels, and the check compares it with the loops.
Notes. Do not write the line for the pixels. The block has the groups write it, and the check tells them which array to transpose.

Repaint the image: a small network

Prob = softmax_rows(layer(X, W, b) / T)    # n rows and K columns
new = Prob @ PAINT                         # n rows and 3 columns
  • Each neuron gets a paint, a colour of the group's choice: the rows of PAINT, K × 3. Prob @ PAINT is n × 3: the new colour of a pixel is a mixture of the K paints, each counted with the probability of its neuron.
  • The second product is of the same kind as the first: n points, now with K coordinates, and three neurons. Two layers with a function between them are a small neural network, applied to all the pixels at once.
Notes. At temperature 1 the picture is nearly one flat colour; at 0.002 every pixel takes the paint of its nearest colour.
